Architecture Decision Record (ADR) — a short, durable document that captures an important architecture decision and its rationale.
Architecture Decision (AD) — a software design choice that is hard to reverse or has significant structural impact.
MADR — Markdown Architecture Decision Records, a popular lightweight, template-driven ADR format.
Context — the forces, constraints, and situation that make a decision necessary.
Consequences — the resulting context after the decision: benefits, costs, and trade-offs.
Supersession — replacing an ADR with a new one (status: Superseded) rather than deleting history.

blocks.text: What is an ADR and why write one?

An Architecture Decision Record is a single, immutable, version-controlled document that records one consequential decision. Architects constantly make choices — which database, which integration style, which framework. Without a record, the "why" evaporates when the original authors leave. ADRs make decisions explicit, reviewable, and reversible-by-design. They are cheap to write (a page or two) and live in the same repository as the code, so the knowledge travels with the system.

A minimal ADR contains a title, a status (Proposed, Accepted, Deprecated, Superseded), the Context describing the problem and constraints, the Decision itself, and the Consequences (positive and negative). Options considered are often summarized to show the decision was not arbitrary. Storing ADRs in git gives you a timestamped audit trail and pull-request review.

The MADR (Markdown ADR) template formalizes this with numbered files (0001-use-postgres.md), a decision drivers section, considered options with pros/cons, and an outcome. It encourages consistency across teams and is the de-facto open standard.

Write one whenever a decision is architecturally significant: it affects structure, cross-team contracts, security, or cost, and is costly to change later. Do not write ADRs for trivial or easily reversible choices. Common triggers: selecting a messaging backbone, choosing eventual vs strong consistency, adopting a new framework, or defining a service boundary.

blocks.value:
# 3. Use Kafka for inter-service events
## Status: Accepted
## Context: We need async, replayable event distribution across 8 services.
## Decision: Adopt Apache Kafka as the central event backbone.
## Consequences: + replayability, + decoupling; - operational complexity, - learning curve.

flowchart LR
    A[Problem / Force] --> B{Architecturally Significant?}
    B -- No --> C[Document in code/README]
    B -- Yes --> D[Write ADR: Context]
    D --> E[ADR: Decision + Options]
    E --> F[ADR: Consequences]
    F --> G[Status: Accepted]
    G --> H[PR Review + Merge]
    H --> I[Future: Supersede if needed]
